title: Nepal trekking permits, TIMS and guide rules
meta_description: Nepal trekking permits for 2026: ACAP, Sagarmatha park and Khumbu fees, TIMS, Upper Mustang restricted permit and licensed-guide rules, with SAARC rates.
summary: Every popular trek in Nepal needs at least one permit. The Annapurna treks need the ACAP permit; Everest needs the Sagarmatha National Park entry and a Khumbu municipality fee; Upper Mustang adds a restricted-area permit through an agency. Since 2023 most foreign trekkers must walk with a licensed guide. Rules change often: check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Why the rules keep changing
paras: Trekking regulation in Nepal is shared between several bodies. The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation runs national parks such as Sagarmatha. The National Trust for Nature Conservation manages the Annapurna Conservation Area. The Department of Immigration issues restricted-area permits for border regions like Upper Mustang. The Nepal Tourism Board and the Trekking Agencies' Association of Nepal run the TIMS system, and since 2017 local rural municipalities have collected their own fees in some areas, most visibly in the Khumbu.

Each of these bodies can change fees or rules on its own timetable, and they do. In the last few years Nepal has introduced a licensed-guide requirement for foreign trekkers, changed how TIMS cards are issued, and revised the Upper Mustang permit. This guide sets out the rules as we understand them for 2026. Treat every number here as indicative and check current status before you travel, ideally with your agency or the Nepal Tourism Board office in Kathmandu or Pokhara.

sections.heading: The licensed-guide rule
paras: From 1 April 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board announced that foreign trekkers in the country's national parks and conservation areas must be accompanied by a licensed guide arranged through a registered trekking agency. The aim was to improve safety after several cases of solo trekkers going missing, and to give more work to Nepali guides. The rule ended most independent trekking on the Annapurna routes in its first season.

The Khumbu works differently. The Khumbu Pasang Lhamu rural municipality, which governs the Everest region, announced that it would not enforce the national guide rule within its area in the same way, and independent trekkers have continued to walk there, paying the local fee at Lukla or Monjo. The position has shifted more than once since 2023.

How the rule applies to Indian nationals has also varied in practice. Some checkpoints have treated Indians like other foreigners, others have not. We include a licensed guide on every trek we sell, because it removes the uncertainty at checkpoints and because a good guide watches for altitude symptoms, finds rooms in busy weeks and knows when the weather will turn. If you plan to walk on your own, check current status before you travel.
list: A licensed guide costs about ₹2,500–3,500 a day on the main trails in 2026, plus their food and room, which lodges often give at a low rate.
A porter costs about ₹1,800–2,500 a day and carries up to 15–20 kg; a porter-guide does both with a lighter load.
Book through a registered agency; your guide should carry a government-issued licence card.

sections.heading: TIMS: what changed
paras: TIMS, the Trekkers' Information Management System, was set up so the authorities know who is on which trail, useful in rescues and after disasters. For years there were two versions: a cheaper blue card for trekkers going with an agency and a green card for independent trekkers. With the licensed-guide requirement, the independent card fell away, and TIMS is now normally issued through your agency as part of your permit package.

In 2023 the TIMS fee for foreign trekkers was set at NPR 2,000, with a lower rate for SAARC nationals. TIMS is required for the Annapurna treks in most cases. In the Khumbu, the local municipality fee replaced TIMS for the Everest region in 2018. For Upper Mustang, your agency handles everything together with the restricted-area permit. Ask your agency exactly which documents you will carry, and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Upper Mustang: the restricted-area permit
paras: Upper Mustang, the old kingdom of Lo north of Kagbeni, is one of Nepal's restricted areas. Foreign nationals, including Indian citizens, need a special permit issued by the Department of Immigration through a registered trekking agency. You must travel with a licensed guide, and the permit is usually issued only to groups of at least two trekkers, though a solo trekker can sometimes be grouped with others by an agency. You also need the ACAP permit.

For many years the permit cost USD 500 for the first 10 days and USD 50 for each extra day, which made short visits expensive. From November 2025 Nepal moved to a daily rate of about USD 50, making a 5–7 day jeep trip to Lo Manthang more affordable. The permit is checked at Kagbeni, so leave plenty of time if you are trying to reach Lo Manthang for the Tiji festival in May. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Insurance and rescue: the permit you forget
paras: No Nepali permit requires travel insurance, but every reputable agency will ask for it on high treks, and you should not walk above 3,000 m without it. A helicopter evacuation from the Khumbu or Upper Mustang can cost several thousand US dollars, and helicopters will not fly until someone guarantees payment. Many standard Indian travel policies exclude trekking above a set altitude, so read the small print.

Look for a policy that names trekking, states a height limit above the highest point of your route, and covers helicopter evacuation and repatriation. Carry the policy number and the insurer's emergency line on paper as well as on your phone, and give a copy to your guide. Talk to your doctor before any trek that sleeps above 3,000 m.

sections.heading: How to get your permits
paras: For trekking with an agency, which is now the normal case, your agency collects your passport details and photos and gets the ACAP permit, TIMS and any restricted-area permit before you start. For the Everest region, the Sagarmatha National Park entry is bought at the park counter in Monjo, and the municipality fee at Lukla or Monjo; your guide handles both on the trail.

If you need to buy an ACAP permit yourself, for example for a short day walk, the Nepal Tourism Board offices in Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, and Damside, Pokhara, issue them on working days. Bring your passport and two passport photos, and pay in Nepali rupees.
list: Carry your passport on the trek; permits are checked at Birethanti, Ghorepani, Monjo, Kagbeni and other points.
Keep paper permits dry in a plastic sleeve; photocopies are useful but checkers want originals.
Do not leave the route named on a restricted-area permit; fines and deportation are possible.
Keep the receipts for fees; you may be asked for them at more than one checkpoint.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for the Poon Hill trek?
faqs.a: You need the Annapurna Conservation Area permit: NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals including Indians, NPR 3,000 for other foreigners, in recent years. TIMS is usually arranged by your agency. Since 2023 a licensed guide is required for most foreign trekkers. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: You need the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit and the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu rural municipality fee. Both are paid on the trail, at Monjo and Lukla, or through your agency. The national TIMS card is not used in the Khumbu. SAARC nationals pay lower rates. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a guide to trek in Nepal?
faqs.a: Nepal's 2023 rule requires foreign trekkers in protected areas to walk with a licensed guide. Enforcement for Indian citizens has varied by checkpoint and year, and the Khumbu has applied its own rules. Our view: hire a licensed guide, which is safer and avoids problems. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a licensed trekking guide cost in Nepal?
faqs.a: About ₹2,500–3,500 a day in 2026 on the main trails, plus the guide's food and lodging, which lodges usually provide at low rates. Shared between two or three trekkers, that adds roughly ₹1,000–1,800 a day each. Tips at the end of a trek are customary.

faqs.q: Is TIMS still required in Nepal?
faqs.a: For the Annapurna region, TIMS is usually still required and is issued through your agency. In the Everest region, the Khumbu municipality fee replaced it in 2018. Fees and requirements have changed several times since 2023, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the Upper Mustang permit for Indians?
faqs.a: Indian citizens pay the same restricted-area permit fee as other foreigners. From November 2025 it moved to about USD 50 a day, replacing the old USD 500 for 10 days. You also need the ACAP permit, a licensed guide and an agency booking, usually with at least two trekkers. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I trek solo in Nepal?
faqs.a: Not independently on most routes: since 2023, foreign trekkers in protected areas need a licensed guide. A solo trekker can still go with a private guide, which is a good option for women travelling alone. The Khumbu has had different rules. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do I get the ACAP permit?
faqs.a: Your trekking agency usually arranges it. You can also buy it at the Nepal Tourism Board offices in Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, and Damside, Pokhara, on working days, with your passport and two photos. Fees are paid in Nepali rupees.

faqs.q: What happens if I trek without a permit?
faqs.a: Checkpoints on all major trails inspect permits. Without one, you will usually be charged double the fee on the spot or turned back, and in restricted areas you can face larger fines or deportation. It is not worth the risk, and the fees support the conservation areas and local communities.
